title: Savitri's vow
hookLine: Savitri fasts three nights, then follows Death; why a Hindu fast is a vow
carry: a fast is a vow, chosen with love
last: SUN SALUTATION — SURYA NAMASKAR IS A BOW TO THE SUN.

lines: DEATH WALKS OUT OF THE TREES.
cards: A princess named Savitri chooses her own husband: Satyavan, an exiled prince living in the forest. Then a sage warns her: he will die in exactly one year. She marries him anyway, and counts the days.
Three days before the end, she makes a vow. For three days and nights she will fast and stand, without rest. On the last morning she follows Satyavan into the forest.
He lays his head in her lap. And Yama, the lord of death, walks out of the trees with his noose.

teach.b: Yama takes Satyavan's life, and Savitri follows him. He tells her to turn back. She keeps walking, and speaks so wisely that he offers her gifts, anything but her husband's life.
Sight for her blind father-in-law. His lost kingdom. Sons for her own father.
Then she asks for a hundred sons, by Satyavan. Yama grants it, and now he has to give Satyavan back. That's the Mahabharata's story.

teach.h: VRATA — A VOW, NOT JUST A FAST.
teach.b: In parts of India married women still keep a fast for Savitri, called Vat Savitri, at a banyan tree. Her three nights were a vrata: a vow. That's the teaching.
In Hindu practice a fast is often one way of keeping a vow, a promise made for a purpose, for a set time, often to a form of God.
Mondays, for many, are for Shiva. The nine nights of Navaratri. And in three days you'll meet the eleventh day of the moon.
Ways to keep one differ: only fruit and milk, one simple meal, no grains, and at the strictest, no water.
Another word for fasting, upavasa, is explained as staying near: near God, near the purpose. The hunger becomes a bell. Every time your stomach speaks, you remember why you chose this.
Children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused, because a fast that harms the body breaks the line from two days ago: the body is a temple.
So when a coworker skips the office pizza for her Monday fast, she isn't being punished.

teach.h: A FAST IS A VOW, CHOSEN WITH LOVE.
teach.b: She's keeping a promise, chosen, with love.

how: Many Hindus keep vratas, vows that often include fasting, on particular weekdays, festivals or lunar days (and some married women keep Vat Savitri, honoring Savitri's vow): some eat only fruit and milk, some one meal, some abstain from grains, and a few go without water; children, elders, the sick and pregnant women are commonly excused.

games.q: Nani is keeping her monday fast, and by afternoon she's hungry. in a vrata, what is that hunger for?
o: it's a punishment for something she did.
it's a bell that brings her back to the vow she chose.
it's a sign she should give up.
games.why: a vrata is a chosen promise. the hunger isn't punishment; it keeps calling her back to the purpose, as Savitri's did.

practice: No fasting required, and if food is complicated for you, leave food out of this completely.

Choose one small thing to skip for the rest of today: a snack, sugar in your tea, or something that isn't food at all, like an hour of scrolling. Then give it a purpose. If you pray, offer it to the form of God you love.
If you don't, offer it for someone you love, the way Savitri did. When you miss it later, let that bring you back.

wordCard.voice: Vrata. A vow: a promise kept for a purpose and a set time, often by fasting, like Savitri's three nights. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit vrata: a vow, a religious observance; often a fast. In Hindi, vrat.

carryVoice: Your line: a fast is a vow, chosen with love. Savitri chose hers, and walked after Death. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.
